speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: The focus is on competencies at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: CET, on the other hand, is often more beneficial to the individual as it imparts skills and competencies which he can use at his workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Singapore is one of the few countries in the world that takes a lifelong learning approach and organises this within one Ministry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: For PET, most primary and secondary schools require minimal co-payment of school fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Higher education at the Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs), polytechnics and autonomous universities also attract significant funding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Students who need additional help can further apply for bursaries and financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: CET is also funded substantially, but with greater gradation depending on the context and outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: For example, for a Professional Conversion Programme, which we are placing a displaced worker into a new industry, we fund it most generously, including wages, while he is undergoing training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: We also provide more support to training of workers in small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: Other training programmes may be funded at up to 70% to help defray the cost of training that can help a company or worker derive individual benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: While this is the broad consideration, the division between PET and CET is never neat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: For example, adult learners may decide to attend full-time Nitec or polytechnic diploma programmes, while an individual who did not attend many years of formal education may undergo CET programmes as part of his formative education and skills upgrading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: The integration of SkillsFuture Singapore into the Ministry of Education (MOE) has raised the awareness of these complexities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Education)
text: By and large, the system is conceptually sound, and we will iron out the arrangements over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Essentially, it is a broader policy question with regard to how the Government is signalling our efforts to develop the culture of continuous learning in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But also, at the back of it, is actually due to some of my recent visits to ITE, talking to the teachers and students.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They shared that there has been a rising number, as the Senior Minister of State has alluded to earlier, a rising number of adult learners going to Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and ITE.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And with regard to recent speeches by Dr Amy Khor, Senior Minister of State for the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources and the Ministry of Health in 2016, she highlighted this close linkage between PET and CET when she went to the Chemical Process Technology Centre (CPCT) where there was a Workforce Development Agency allocation of $8 million and 1,650 Post-Secondary Education Institution (PSEI) students actually benefited from these CPCT arrangement over three years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the Government has actually worked to merge PET and CET together in some small cases like this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was wondering what more can the Government do in terms of signalling more about how we can actually merge PET and CET in some grey areas or, in the future, what are the long-term strategies that Government plans to do, particularly in the sense of developing a culture of continuous learning in Singapore, going forward?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Member is right that the culture of lifelong learning does not stop at learning in school or in the IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: After the individual has left the IHLs, left school, we want this learning to continue for life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And that is why the lines between education institutions and workplace need to be further blurred so that for someone in school, in an IHL, we want to bring workplace requirements and workplace experiences into our schools and into our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Internships, job relevant skills – these are elements which we want to be able to bring into our schools and our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to be able to bring our workers who have already started work, who have already left school, to go back and do further upgrading of skills, lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why the direction that MOE has taken in recent years is to encourage our IHLs to not only focus on providing PET but to also look at being providers of CET and make that a core part of their mission.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we can do it this way, we are then able to have this two-way flow – what the workplace requires in terms of skills and experience, bring it into the schools and IHLs, and to be able to also bring our workers back to reskill, to upskill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to continue to nurture and treasure this very strong partnership that we have built up over the years because it is very helpful.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When it comes to retraining, we need the workers to be onboard, the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also need the employers to be on board and that is why the Government, together with employers and union, we will continue to work on this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because this is, as the Member said, a lifelong pursuit, changing the culture, making lifelong learning part of our DNA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For adult Singaporeans who want to pursue a second or third degree in, for example, skills that are in demand, like cybersecurity, data analytics, occupational therapy, speech pathology, do they get to receive subsidised fees when they enter our local universities?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have the impression that they are not; they do not get that because it is another bite of the cherry, depending on how many times they have received a subsidy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And if they do not get a subsidy, then, why not, because these skills are in demand?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, we want to provide opportunities for adult learners who want to switch careers and who want to pick up a new skill, to be able to go through such lifelong learning and skills upgrading programmes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, what we have provided are various schemes under the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, these are all different schemes that the Government has provided to help our workers who need to pick up a new skill to be able to transit to a new career or, sometimes, just to pick up additional skills to do their current jobs in their current industries – do it at a higher level, do it better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we will look at such ways to support.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you join one of these programmes, there will be additional subsidies up to 90%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It also depends on the profile of the employer and the profile of the worker.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Older workers, as well as workers who are working in SMEs, we do provide more funding support.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, to answer Ms Denise Phua's question, the evolution of these various courses has to move in tandem with what the economy requires.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when there are new requirements, there are new skills required, there will be new courses that will be added to the list and new courses that can be funded as part of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is something which I think we will continuously look at to see what we can do to continue to support our workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you can keep it brief, Dr Intan Mokhtar.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Following up on the hon Ms Denise Phua's question is that, increasingly, the lines between CET and PET are being blurred.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, increasingly, more IHLs are introducing stackable modules or stackable courses that lead to a qualification like a diploma or degree.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, how then do you reconcile the funding models between PET and CET?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because you can have someone who already has a degree, but through stackable modules, you can get another degree, eventually.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the resources that we have are limited.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when you divert resources into one area, it means you have less resources for another area.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Or, if they have a polytechnic diploma, they are going for a degree, how do we help them, in areas that are relevant to their work, to be able to do so?
